question.explanation:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block $J_n(\lambda),$ we have \[ f(J_n(\lambda)) = \begin{bmatrix} f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \dfrac{f''(\lambda)}{2!} & \cdots & \dfrac{f^{(n-1)}(\lambda)}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) & \cdots & \dfrac{f^{(n-2)}(\lambda)}{(n-2)!} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & f(\lambda) & f'(\lambda) \\ 0 & \cdots & \cdots & 0 & f(\lambda) \end{bmatrix}. \]

In this case, we have $f(x) = x^3,$ $n=2,$ and $\lambda=5.$ Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first $2-1=1$ derivatives of $f{:}$ \begin{align*} f(x) &= x^3 \\[5pt] f'(x) &= 3x^2 \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \begin{align*} f\left(J_2\left(5\right)\right) &= \begin{bmatrix} f\left(5\right) & f'\left(5\right) \\ 0 & f\left(5\right) \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 5^3 & 3\cdot5^2 \\ 0 & 5^3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{125} & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{75} \\ \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0} & \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{125} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

question.text:
Consider the following matrices:

\[ C = \begin{bmatrix} \pi &2\pi \\ 0&2\pi \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{bmatrix} \pi &0 \\ 0 & 2\pi \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Given that $C = PDP^{-1},$ find $\cos C.$
question.explanation:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have \[ f(SAS^{-1}) = S \cdot f(A) \cdot S^{-1}. \]

For $f(x) =\cos C$ and the given matrix $C,$ we have

\[ \cos C = \cos (PDP^{-1}) = P \cdot (\cos D) \cdot P^{-1}. \]

Now, since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we get

\[ \cos D = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \pi & 0\\ 0 & \cos 2\pi \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

\[ P^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{1\cdot1 - 2\cdot 0} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \cos C &= P \cdot (\cos D) \cdot P^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -1&2\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -1&4\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text:
Consider the following matrices:

\[ E = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad J = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \]

Given that $E = PJP^{-1},$ find $\cos(\pi E).$
question.explanation:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have \[ f(SAS^{-1}) = S \cdot f(A) \cdot S^{-1}. \]

For $f(x) = \cos(\pi x)$ and the given matrix $E,$ we have

\[ \cos(\pi E) = \cos\left(\pi{PJP^{-1}}\right) = P \cdot (\cos{\pi J}) \cdot P^{-1}. \]

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $2$s on the main diagonal, we have

\[ f(J) = \begin{bmatrix} f(2) & f'(2) \\ 0 & f(2) \end{bmatrix}. \]

The derivative of $f$ is $f'(x) = -\pi \sin(\pi x).$ So, we get

\[ \cos(\pi E) = \begin{bmatrix} f(2) & f'(2) \\ 0 & f(2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(2\pi) & -\pi \sin(2\pi) \\ 0 &\cos(2\pi) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

\[ P^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{1\cdot3 - 1\cdot2} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 &-2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, we conclude that

\begin{align*} cos(\pi E) &= P \cdot (\cos(\pi J)) \cdot P^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 &-2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 &-2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}
